prompt:
A tissue engineering company is developing a biodegradable scaffold for full-thickness dermal wound healing. The scaffold is fabricated from electrospun polycaprolactone (PCL) with a fibre diameter of 500 nanometres, forming a non-woven mesh with a mean pore size of 5 micrometres and porosity of 85%. The scaffold is 2 mm thick and intended for application to chronic diabetic foot ulcers.

The design rationale states that PCL was selected for its slow degradation profile, with an expected in vivo degradation time of 24-36 months, ensuring the scaffold maintains mechanical support throughout the wound healing process. The engineering team notes that dermal wound healing in diabetic patients typically completes within 12-16 weeks, and the scaffold's persistence beyond this period provides a safety margin for delayed healing.

The scaffold has been evaluated per ISO 10993-1 for biocompatibility (surface device, prolonged contact). In vitro cell culture studies demonstrate fibroblast adhesion and proliferation on the scaffold surface. Mechanical testing shows the scaffold tensile strength exceeds the native dermis (15 MPa vs approximately 10 MPa for human dermis). The product is sterilised by gamma irradiation at 25 kGy per ISO 11137. The regulatory submission classifies the device as a Class II wound dressing under FDA 21 CFR 878.4018.

seeded_faults.description: The PCL scaffold has a degradation time of 24-36 months, but the target wound healing completes in 12-16 weeks (3-4 months). A scaffold persisting 6-9 times longer than the healing period is not a safety margin — it is a foreign body that will provoke chronic inflammatory response. Once the wound has re-epithelialised, the remaining scaffold acts as a persistent foreign body, triggering giant cell formation, fibrous encapsulation, and chronic inflammation that can impair the quality of the healed tissue and cause patient discomfort. Ideal scaffold degradation should match or slightly exceed the tissue regeneration timeline. FDA Guidance 'Regulatory Considerations for Human Cells, Tissues, and Cellular and Tissue-Based Products' and ISO 10993-9 (degradation testing for absorbable materials) both establish that degradation-tissue remodelling temporal matching is a fundamental design requirement.
seeded_faults.location_hint: PCL degradation time of 24-36 months vs 12-16 week healing period

seeded_faults.description: The scaffold has a mean pore size of 5 micrometres. Published literature on tissue engineering scaffolds for dermal regeneration consistently demonstrates that pore sizes of 100-250 micrometres are required for cell infiltration, vascularisation, and tissue ingrowth (Yannas et al., 1989; Murphy et al., 2010; Loh & Choong, 2013). At 5 micrometres, the pores are too small for fibroblast migration (fibroblasts are 10-15 micrometres in diameter) and far too small for capillary ingrowth (minimum approximately 30-50 micrometres). The scaffold would function as a surface barrier rather than a three-dimensional tissue engineering construct. While the in vitro data shows fibroblast adhesion and proliferation on the surface, cells cannot infiltrate the scaffold volume. This renders the 2 mm thickness functionally useless as a tissue scaffold, making it an occlusive wound dressing at best.

ground_truth_notes: Scaffold pore size requirements for dermal regeneration per Yannas et al. (1989) Science, Murphy et al. (2010) Biomaterials, and Loh & Choong (2013) Tissue Engineering Part B. Cell size data: human dermal fibroblasts 10-15 um diameter (Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell). Minimum capillary diameter approximately 5-10 um, but capillary ingrowth into scaffolds requires pores of 30-50+ um (Druecke et al., 2004). PCL degradation kinetics per Woodruff & Hutmacher (2010) Progress in Polymer Science. ISO 10993-9:2019 covers biological evaluation of degradation products from absorbable medical devices. Foreign body response to persistent implants per Anderson et al. (2008) Seminars in Immunology.
